newsitem.title: INDIA: Blast kills at least 300 on Indian train - police.
newsitem.headline: Blast kills at least 300 on Indian train - police.

text.p: At least 300 people were believed to have been killed when a powerful bomb ripped through several carriages of a packed train in India's northeastern state of Assam on Monday, police said.

Immediately after the attack up to 40 bodies were recovered from the mangled wreckage but then darkness fell on the remote area and further rescue work had to wait until lighting was brought to the site.
The final death count is expected to be much higher, local railway officials said.
The Press Trust of India news agency quoted officials as saying the death toll was at least 300.

A senior police official told Reuters in Assam's biggest city of Guwahati that suspected separatist Bodo militants had used a remote-controlled device packed with explosives to blow up the Delhi-bound Brahmaputra Mail.
If police fears are realised it would make the attack the second most devastating guerrilla action on record.
In June 1985, Sikh extremists were blamed for a bomb on an Air India Boeing 747 which crashed into the sea off Ireland, killing 329 people.
In December 1988, 270 died when a bomb destroyed a Pan American Boeing 747 over the Scottish town of Lockerbie.
Around 1,000 people were travelling ahead of the New Year holiday on the express train, named after the sacred river that flows through India's northeast.
"Bodo guerrillas blew up three coaches of a passenger train killing at least 300 people at Sensapani railway station," the police official told Reuters.
Sensapani is 200 km (125 miles) west of Guwahati, hub of the oil-producing and tea-rich state, seven kilometres west of Kokrajhar, a centre of Bodo separatist activity.
The train had left Kokrajhar for Delhi around 7 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Monday. It consisted of about 15 carriages, each one crammed with between 75 and 100 people.

One of the coaches torn apart by the blast was an air-conditioned carriage with reserved seats but another was for passengers without reservations and was thought to be carrying far more than its capacity.
The third carriage was a restaurant car and railway officials fear that an explosion of gas cylinders aboard this car may have caused more deaths.
Police and local residents in the town of Kokrajhar said they heard two loud explosions.
A police and medical team reached the site of the devastation in pitch darkness around midnight (1830 GMT) and had to set up emergency lighting before rescue operations could resume.
Sixteen survivors walked three kilometres (two miles) to the next station on the line at Fakiragram.
Describing the explosion, the police official said: "They used RDX (research and development plastic explosives) and a remote-controlled device."
RDX became widely known in India after it was used in a series of bomb blasts that killed 260 people in Bombay in March, 1993.
The attack came a day after tribal Bodo guerrillas blew up a road bridge that formed the main link between India's northeast regions and the rest of the country, injuring seven people.

Activists representing Bodo tribesmen living north of the Brahmaputra river want a homeland within India in the state of Assam, but an extremist fringe, the Bodoland Army, has been fighting for a separate nation since 1989.
Bodo guerrillas have carried out ambushes, kidnappings and attacked railway lines in the past.

"This is the worst incident of separatist violence in Assam this year," the police official said. Most of the passengers were believed to be holiday-makers heading for Delhi to celebrate the New Year.
Police said none of the several guerrillas groups operating in Assam had claimed responsibility for the blast.
More than 5,000 people have been killed in ethnic and separatist violence in Assam during the last three years.
Militants of the Maoist United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA) have frequently targeted Indian security personnel in the region.
United News of India newsagency said Bodo extremists had killed 1,000 people since their violent campaign for independence began in 1989.
